name: Separation from LCMS
description: AELC formed in 1976 after separating from the LCMS.
narrative: AELC formed in 1976 after separating from the LCMS. The AELC emerged from severe conflict within the Missouri Synod over theology and institutional direction. It provided an organizational home for departing congregations and became a partner in discussions for a new Lutheran church. Though much smaller than the ALC and LCA, it was a full participant in the resulting ELCA. A fuller account needs primary records of the dispute rather than a one-sided label about which party preserved Lutheranism.

key_figures.name: William Kohn
key_figures.summary: A Lutheran pastor and former LCMS mission executive elected president when the AELC was constituted in late 1976. Contemporary reporting connects his departure from Missouri Synod leadership to the conflict over its conservative direction.

key_figures.name: Will Herzfeld
key_figures.summary: An Oakland pastor and Black Lutheran leader elected vice-president at the AELC’s founding convention, participating in the creation of an organizational home for departing congregations.

name: Merger into ELCA
description: ALC merged into the ELCA effective January 1, 1988, following the 1987 constituting convention.
narrative: ALC merged into the ELCA effective January 1, 1988, following the 1987 constituting convention. The merger brought together multiple strands of North American Lutheran history, including immigrant churches and the AELC’s more recent division from the Missouri Synod. Its constituting convention in April 1987 elected Herbert Chilstrom; operations began January 1, 1988. The distinction reconciles official descriptions that use either a constituting year or a startup year. The ELCA’s identity joins Lutheran confession with an extensive network of ministries and ecumenical relationships.
